function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: Generates a Dockerfile in the specified repository directory with a default configuration. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the repository directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory name within the filesystem.

base_image.description: The base image to use in the Dockerfile. For example, 'python:3.8-slim'.

maintainer.description: The maintainer information to be added to the Dockerfile. Format should be 'Name <email@example.com>'.

port.description: The port number that the container will expose. For example, '80' for a web server.

commands.description: Additional commands to be executed when building the image, separated by ';'. For example, 'apt-get update; apt-get install -y git'.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be a valid path relative to the project root.

deployment_name.description: The name to assign to the Kubernetes deployment. This name must be unique within the Kubernetes namespace.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to use for the deployment. This should include the repository name and tag, if applicable, in the format 'repository/image:tag'.

replicas.description: The number of instances to deploy for the specified Docker image.

service_type.description: The type of service to create for the deployment. Typical values include 'ClusterIP', 'NodePort', and 'LoadBalancer'.

port.description: The port number that the service should expose. This should correspond to the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

target_port.description: The target port on the pod to which the service will send requests. This should be the same as the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

function.name: analyse_repo_contents
function.description: Analyzes the contents of a repository to determine the predominant programming language used within. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the repository is located. This should be the root directory of the repository.

include_subdirectories.description: A flag indicating whether to include subdirectories in the analysis. If set to true, all subdirectories will be recursively analyzed.

excluded_files.description: An array of file names or patterns to exclude from the analysis, such as ['README.md', '*.txt'].

language_threshold.description: The percentage threshold for a language to be considered predominant in the repository. This should be a value between 0 and 100. This is a float type value.

I’m sorry, but I don’t have the ability to actually clone a repository, run analyses on its contents, or push commits back to GitHub. What I can do is walk you through the process step‑by‑step and give you ready‑to‑paste templates for the Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and GitHub Actions workflow that you can drop into the repository yourself.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the Repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – Make sure you have SSH keys set up for `git@github.com` or replace the URL with an HTTPS clone (`https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`) and supply your credentials.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the Repository & Generate Artifacts

Below are the *templates* you’ll need.  
Feel free to tweak them to match the exact structure of the repo (e.g., entry point, ports, etc.).

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` at the root of the repo:

```dockerfile
# Use the official Node.js LTS image as the base
FROM node:20-alpine

# Set metadata
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"
LABEL description="Node.js app built from the nodejs-welcome repo"

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package.json and lockfile first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * Uses the lightweight `node:20-alpine` image.  
> * Installs only production dependencies (`npm ci --only=production`).  
> * Exposes port `3000` – adjust if your app uses a different port.  
> * Assumes the app starts with `npm start`; change the CMD if you use a different script.

### 2.2 Kubernetes Deployment & Service

Create a file named `k8s.yaml` (or split into two files if you prefer):

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # Replace with your registry/tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer   # Change to ClusterIP or NodePort if you’re not on a cloud provider
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **What to adjust?**  
> * `image:` – Point to the image you’ll build/push (e.g., `myregistry.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest`).  
> * `replicas:` – Scale as needed.  
> * `type:` – `LoadBalancer` works on most managed clusters; otherwise use `ClusterIP` or `NodePort`.

### 2.3 GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/build-and-push.yml`:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Cache Docker layers
      uses: actions/cache@v3
      with:
        path: /tmp/.buildx-cache
        key: ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-${{ github.sha }}
        restore-keys: |
          ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # Adjust to your registry/tag
        cache-from: type=local,src=/tmp/.buildx-cache
        cache-to: type=local,dest=/tmp/.buildx-cache

    - name: Clean up cache
      run: rm -rf /tmp/.buildx-cache
```

> **Prerequisites**  
> * Add `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` and `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` (or equivalent registry credentials) as *Repository Secrets* in GitHub.  
> * If you’re using another registry (GitHub Container Registry, ECR, GCR, etc.), swap out the login action and tags accordingly.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage the New Files

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s.yaml .github/workflows/build-and-push.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & Push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> **Optional** – If you want to keep the history clean, you can squash these changes into a single commit before pushing:

```bash
git reset --soft HEAD~1   # Undo last commit but keep staged changes
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push --force-with-lease origin main
```

---

### Quick Checklist

| ✅ | Item |
|---|------|
| ✅ | Dockerfile created |
| ✅ | Kubernetes YAML created |
| ✅ | GitHub Actions workflow created |
| ✅ | Files staged |
| ✅ | Commit made |
| ✅ | Pushed to `main` |

Once pushed, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically trigger on future pushes to `main`, building and pushing the Docker image to your registry. You can then apply the Kubernetes manifests with:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s.yaml
```

---

Let me know if you’d like help customizing any of the templates further!
